ai.definition: Carbon-negative concrete is a type of concrete that incorporates captured carbon dioxide (CO2) to form calcium carbonate through mineralization processes.
ai.howItWorks: During production, CO2 is injected into the concrete mix. The CO2 reacts with the cement paste and other minerals in the mixture, forming stable calcium carbonate structures which permanently trap the CO2 within the concrete matrix. This process not only reduces atmospheric CO2 levels but also enhances the compressive strength of the resulting material.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing climate change by reducing CO2 emissions and sequestering carbon dioxide while improving structural properties of traditional concrete.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves capturing CO2 from industrial sources or direct air capture, then injecting it into a concrete mixture. This requires specialized equipment for CO2 injection and handling, as well as additional steps in the curing process to ensure complete mineralization.
ai.buildProcess: Similar to conventional concrete, but with an added step of CO2 injection during mixing. The concrete is then cured under controlled conditions to allow for full mineralization of the incorporated CO2.
ai.costDrivers: High initial costs due to specialized equipment and processes required for CO2 capture and injection. Energy-intensive manufacturing process due to vacuum baking requirements, which can significantly increase overall production costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected growth as more carbon capture technologies become available and the demand for sustainable construction materials increases.
ai.regulation: Currently no specific regulations exist for carbon-negative concrete. However, it is likely to be subject to future environmental standards related to CO2 sequestration and sustainability in construction.
ai.risks: Technical risks associated with ensuring complete mineralization of injected CO2 and maintaining structural integrity over time. Economic risks due to high initial costs and potential market volatility for carbon capture technologies.
ai.profitability: Uncertain, as the technology is still in its early stages and requires significant investment. Potential long-term benefits from reduced carbon emissions could lead to increased profitability if widely adopted.
ai.futureDevelopment: Continued research into improving CO2 injection methods, enhancing mineralization processes, and reducing manufacturing energy requirements. Integration with other sustainable building materials and practices.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking (high kWh per ton).

glossary.def: The process of capturing carbon dioxide from industrial sources or the atmosphere.
The transformation of CO2 into stable calcium carbonate through chemical reactions within concrete.

subsystems.name: Binder
subsystems.role: the cementitious glue; in a low-carbon mix it replaces most or all Portland clinker.

subsystems.name: Aggregate
subsystems.role: bulk filler, which can itself be a carbonated material made from captured CO2.
parts: crushed steel slag or mine tailings

subsystems.name: CO2 supply
subsystems.role: provides the gas that will be chemically locked into the concrete.
parts: flue-gas capture unit at a kiln, steel mill or refinery

subsystems.name: Injection or curing system
subsystems.role: brings CO2 into contact with the fresh paste so it mineralises as calcium carbonate.
parts: in-line injection manifold for mixing trucks

subsystems.name: Batching and placement
subsystems.role: mixes and places the concrete fast, because carbonation accelerates setting.

subsystems.name: Testing and accounting
subsystems.role: proves the concrete meets structural standards and measures how much CO2 is genuinely bound.

buildSteps.title: Capture the CO2
buildSteps.detail: A concentrated stream is captured from a cement kiln, steel plant or refinery flue gas, then purified and compressed for delivery. Using the kiln's own CO2 closes the loop at the source of most cement emissions.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the binder
buildSteps.detail: Slag, fly ash or calcined clay is ground and blended; a low-lime calcium silicate clinker may replace ordinary Portland clinker. The activator or clinker dose is kept as low as the strength target allows, since activators carry their own emissions.

buildSteps.title: Batch and mix
buildSteps.detail: Binder, aggregate, water and superplasticiser are combined. If carbonation happens in the mixer, CO2 is dosed into the drum under controlled pressure so it reacts with calcium in the paste before the mix stiffens.

buildSteps.title: Place promptly
buildSteps.detail: Concrete is poured into formwork within a shortened working window, because carbonation accelerates setting and reduces slump.

buildSteps.title: Cure under CO2
buildSteps.detail: Precast units go into a sealed chamber where CO2 concentration and pressure are raised for hours to days. The gas diffuses into the paste and reacts with calcium silicates and hydroxide to form stable calcium carbonate.

buildSteps.title: Demould and finish
buildSteps.detail: Forms are stripped and surfaces finished; a period of conventional moist curing may follow to reach the specified strength.

buildSteps.title: Verify strength and storage
buildSteps.detail: Cores are crushed for compressive strength and samples are analysed for carbonate content, so the amount of CO2 chemically locked in is measured rather than assumed.

buildSteps.title: Account and deploy
buildSteps.detail: A life-cycle assessment covering mining, transport, activator production, curing energy and end-of-life is run. Only if stored CO2 exceeds all of those emissions can the product honestly be called carbon-negative.

prerequisites.tech: Low-clinker binders (alkali-activated slag/fly ash, calcined clay)
prerequisites.why: they cut the calcination emissions that make up most of cement's footprint, but are not yet permitted by every structural code.

prerequisites.tech: CO2 capture from industrial flue gas
prerequisites.why: amine scrubbing and similar processes operate commercially in other industries; fitting them to cement kilns is only now beginning.
CO2 reacting with calcium and magnesium silicates to form permanent carbonates is well understood and demonstrated, but reaction rates and reactor throughput still limit use.
engineers will not specify a new concrete for bridges and buildings until standards define its strength, durability and testing.
grinding, activating and curing all consume energy; the emissions saved by the chemistry can be given back by a fossil-heavy grid.

pathway.milestone: carbon-cured precast blocks and pavers sold commercially, with CO2 injected during mixing or curing
pathway.unlocks: a working supply chain and a handful of verified tonnes of permanently stored carbon per plant.

pathway.milestone: mineralised aggregate and alkali-activated structural concrete accepted into building codes
pathway.unlocks: replacing clinker in ready-mix and cast-in-place work, where the vast majority of concrete volume sits.

pathway.milestone: batching plants sited beside cement kilns and steel mills and run on their captured flue gas
pathway.unlocks: concrete production turned from a pure emissions source into a modest carbon sink.

pathway.milestone: whole-life carbon accounting that credits the slow natural reabsorption of CO2 by concrete without double-counting
pathway.unlocks: honest, audited net-negative claims and a durable storage route for captured carbon.
